overview.why: "Design a system that serves a million users" is the classic senior-engineer interview question, and it increasingly appears in campus placements too. It is less about one right answer and more about showing that you ask good questions, know the building blocks (load balancers, caches, queues, replicas) and can explain trade-offs out loud.
prerequisites: Networking basics and AWS cloud basics: you will use terms like load balancer, DNS and subnet.
outcomes: Choose between vertical and horizontal scaling and say what each costs
Place a cache (Redis) in front of a database and avoid stale or stampeding data
Scale a database with read replicas, partitioning and sharding
Explain the CAP theorem with a real example and pick consistency or availability on purpose
Use a message queue to smooth traffic and decouple services
overview.placementTip: Follow a simple script in every design answer: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch the big boxes, then dig into the part the interviewer cares about. Talk about trade-offs, not just components.

sections.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

content.value: Imagine you run a pizza delivery store with 1 delivery driver. Traffic spikes on game night. You have two choices: **Scale Vertically** (buy the driver a faster sports car) or **Scale Horizontally** (hire 5 more drivers on bicycles). Buying a faster car has physical limits and costs a fortune. Hiring more drivers scales infinitely!

content.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
content.value:
graph TB
    subgraph VERT ["Vertical Scaling (Scale UP)"]
        V1["🖥️ Small Server (2 CPU, 4GB)"] -->|Upgrade hardware| V2["🖥️ Massive Server (64 CPU, 256GB)"]
        V2 --> LIMIT["⚠️ Physical Hardware & Cost Ceiling"]
    end
    subgraph HORIZ ["Horizontal Scaling (Scale OUT)"]
        H1["🖥️ Server 1"] & H2["🖥️ Server 2"] & H3["🖥️ Server 3"] & H4["🖥️ Server 4"]
        LB["⚖️ Load Balancer"] --> H1 & H2 & H3 & H4
    end
    style VERT fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style HORIZ fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Scaling Comparison Matrix
content.value:
Feature          Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)    Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Strategy         Add more CPU / RAM to 1 machine Add more machines to pool
Downtime         Usually requires reboot        Zero downtime (add/remove nodes)
Cost             Exponentially expensive        Linear & cost-efficient
Fault Tolerance  Single point of failure (SPOF) High availability (N+1 redundancy)
Limit            Strict hardware cap            Virtually unlimited

keyPoints: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger (simple, but it has a ceiling); horizontal adds more machines (needs a load balancer and stateless servers).
Keep servers **stateless**, with sessions and files in shared storage, so any server can handle any request.
Look for the bottleneck before you scale: CPU, memory, disk, network or the database.

quiz.question: What is the primary benefit of Horizontal Scaling over Vertical Scaling?
options: Single servers are easier to manage
High fault tolerance and virtually unlimited elasticity by adding inexpensive commodity nodes
Vertical scaling is cheaper at scale
quiz.explanation: Horizontal scaling distributes traffic across multiple instances. If one node fails, the load balancer redirects traffic to remaining healthy nodes with zero downtime.

sections.title: Caching Strategies (Redis & Memcached)

content.value: Disk read is slow (~10ms). RAM read is blazingly fast (~0.1ms). **Caching** stores frequently queried database results in RAM (using Redis or Memcached) so your database doesn't crash during traffic surges.

content.title: Cache-Aside Strategy Flow
content.value:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client Request
    participant API as Web Server
    participant REDIS as Redis Cache (RAM)
    participant DB as SQL Database (Disk)
    C->>API: GET /user/profile/123
    API->>REDIS: Check key 'user:123'
    alt Cache Hit (95% of requests)
        REDIS->>API: Return JSON from RAM (2ms) ✅
    else Cache Miss (5% of requests)
        REDIS->>API: Key not found ❌
        API->>DB: Query SQL on disk (80ms)
        DB->>API: Return DB record
        API->>REDIS: Save key 'user:123' with TTL 1 hour
    end
    API->>C: Return user data
Cache Invalidation Rule: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Always set a TTL (Time To Live) on cached keys to prevent stale data.

keyPoints: Memory is far faster than disk, so cache what is read often and changes rarely.
Cache-aside: check the cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache.
Decide how data expires (TTL) and how it is invalidated, because stale data is the cost of caching.

quiz.question: In the Cache-Aside pattern, what happens when a request experiences a 'Cache Miss'?
options: The server queries the database, returns data to user, and writes data to cache for future requests
quiz.explanation: On a Cache Miss, the application fetches the data directly from the slow database, populates the cache with that data, and returns the response to the caller.

sections.title: Database Scaling: Replicas & Sharding

content.value: Most web apps do 90% READ operations and 10% WRITE operations. To scale databases:

content.title: Database Read Replicas vs Sharding
content.value:
graph TB
    subgraph RR ["Read Replicas (Scale READS)"]
        M1["👑 Primary Database\n(Handles WRITEs)"] -->|Async Replication| R1["📖 Replica 1 (READs)"]
        M1 -->|Async Replication| R2["📖 Replica 2 (READs)"]
    end
    subgraph SHARD ["Horizontal Sharding (Scale WRITES & STORAGE)"]
        S1["DB Shard 1\nUsers A - M"] & S2["DB Shard 2\nUsers N - Z"]
    end
    style RR fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style SHARD fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

**Read Replicas** — All writes go to the Primary DB. Changes replicate asynchronously to Read Replicas. All SELECT queries hit the replicas.

**Database Sharding** — Splitting a huge table across multiple database servers based on a Shard Key (e.g., User ID % 2).

keyPoints: Most apps read far more than they write: send reads to replicas, writes to the primary.
Replicas can lag behind, so a user may briefly not see their own write.
Sharding splits data across databases by a key; it scales writes but makes queries and joins harder.

quiz.question: Which database pattern is best for handling high write volumes and huge dataset growth beyond a single server disk?
quiz.explanation: Database Sharding partitions data horizontally across multiple independent servers (shards), allowing you to scale both WRITE capacity and storage capacity.

sections.title: CAP Theorem & Message Queues

content.value: The **CAP Theorem** states that a distributed system can only provide TWO of the following three guarantees at the same time:

content.title: CAP Theorem Triangle
content.value:
graph TD
    C["Consistency (C)\nEvery node sees same data"]
    A["Availability (A)\nEvery request gets a response"]
    P["Partition Tolerance (P)\nSystem operates despite network breaks"]
    C --- A
    A --- P
    P --- C
    style C fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style A fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style P fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0

**Message Queues (Kafka / RabbitMQ)** decouple background work. When a user buys a product, the API places a message in the Queue and responds in 20ms. Background workers process email receipts, inventory, and analytics asynchronously.

keyPoints: During a network partition a distributed system must choose consistency or availability.
Banks tend to choose consistency; social feeds tend to choose availability with eventual consistency.
Queues (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ) absorb bursts and let services work at their own pace.

quiz.question: Why do modern microservices use Message Queues (like RabbitMQ / Kafka)?
options: To decouple services and execute heavy background tasks asynchronously without blocking API responses
quiz.explanation: Message queues enable asynchronous communication. The web server enqueues background jobs (sending emails, video processing) and returns a fast response to the user while background workers handle the heavy lifting.

cheatsheet.title: System design cheat sheet
rows: Load balancer
Spreads requests across servers and checks their health
CDN
Serves static files from locations near the user
Cache (Redis)
Fast in-memory store in front of the database
Read replica
Copy of the database that serves reads
Sharding
Splitting data across databases by a key
Message queue
Buffer between producer and consumer services
Rate limiter
Protects a service from too many requests
Idempotency
Doing a request twice has the same result as once
Back-of-envelope
1M users/day is about 12 requests per second on average
Latency numbers
RAM ~0.1 ms, SSD ~0.1-1 ms, same-region network ~1 ms, disk seek ~10 ms
